main.title: Castle of Illusion Starring Mickey Mouse
main.subtitle: A cartoon behind every door
main.summary: Sega’s 1990 Mega Drive adventure sends Mickey Mouse into Mizrabel’s castle to rescue Minnie. Seven Gems of the Rainbow are the key to reaching her. The castle is a framework for different worlds of illusion, turning a familiar rescue story into a succession of forests, oversized toys and enchanted everyday objects.

cards.heading: A cartoon behind every door
cards.text: Sega’s 1990 Mega Drive adventure sends Mickey Mouse into Mizrabel’s castle to rescue Minnie. Seven Gems of the Rainbow are the key to reaching her. The castle is a framework for different worlds of illusion, turning a familiar rescue story into a succession of forests, oversized toys and enchanted everyday objects.

cards.heading: Learning the rhythm of an illusion
cards.text: Mickey can bounce onto enemies or throw collected projectiles, so reading a landing and judging a gap matter as much as moving forward. Floating leaves, toy soldiers and an enormous library give the platforming a changing sense of scale. The original 16-bit game documented here is distinct from the related Master System and Game Gear games, and from the 2013 remake. Sega later included the Mega Drive version in its Mini console, presenting the original sprites and stages again.

main.title: Chip ’n Dale Rescue Rangers
main.subtitle: A rescue team at ground level
main.summary: Capcom’s 1990 NES adventure turns the Rescue Rangers’ small size into a way of seeing the world. A missing kitten draws Chip, Dale and their friends into a city troubled by mechanical bulldogs and robotic rats, with Fat Cat behind the danger. Ordinary crates become weapons or hiding places, and steel boxes can be stacked to reach higher platforms. The action is built around picking up, carrying and throwing objects rather than a permanent weapon: a familiar room becomes an obstacle course when its occupants are only a few centimetres tall.

cards.heading: A city built for giants
cards.text: Capcom’s 1990 NES adventure turns the Rescue Rangers’ small size into a way of seeing the world. cards.heading: Two small heroes, one adventure
cards.text: One player can choose either chipmunk, while two players explore together on the same screen. Gadget prepares inventions and clues, Monterey Jack helps uncover routes, and Zipper provides temporary protection. The manual makes these supporting characters part of the rescue operation rather than simply a television cast on the packaging. Harumi Fujita’s NES score gives the journey its lively musical identity. Capcom later included the original game in The Disney Afternoon Collection in 2017, alongside five other 8-bit Disney adventures.

main.title: Golden Joystick Awards 1990

cards.heading: The players' awards
cards.text: The Golden Joystick Awards celebrate games through a public vote, bringing players into the choice of each year's winners. The awards began in Britain with the 1983 season and later reached an international audience through online voting. Their changing categories trace the growth of games: home computers and consoles, handhelds, online play, independent studios, performance and music. Alongside the public vote, special honours recognise individual contributions to the industry. Each edition preserves its own category names, so the results also show what players and the awards organisers considered worth celebrating at the time.

main.title: The Secret of Monkey Island
main.summary: The Secret of Monkey Island is a 1990 point-and-click graphic adventure game developed and published by Lucasfilm Games.

cards.text: The Secret of Monkey Island is a 1990 point-and-click graphic adventure game developed and published by Lucasfilm Games. It takes place in a fictional version of the Caribbean during the age of piracy. The player assumes the role of Guybrush Threepwood, a young man who dreams of becoming a pirate, and explores fictional islands while solving puzzles.

The game was conceived in 1988 by Lucasfilm employee Ron Gilbert, who designed it with Tim Schafer and Dave Grossman. Gilbert's frustrations with contemporary adventure titles led him to make the player character's death almost impossible, which meant that gameplay focused on exploration. The atmosphere was based on that of the Pirates of the Caribbean theme park ride. The Secret of Monkey Island was the fifth game built with the SCUMM engine, which was heavily modified to include a more user-friendly interface.

Critics praised The Secret of Monkey Island for its humor, audiovisuals, and gameplay. Several publications list it among the greatest video games of all time. The game spawned a number of sequels, collectively known as the Monkey Island series. Gilbert, Schafer and Grossman also led the development of the sequel Monkey Island 2: LeChuck's Revenge. LucasArts released a remake of the original in 2009, which was also well received by the gaming press.

cards.heading: How insult sword fighting was written
cards.text: Gilbert soon realised that it would be difficult to design the game by himself; he decided to join forces with Tim Schafer and Dave Grossman, both of whom he hired for Lucasfilm. The game's insult sword fighting mechanics were influenced by swashbuckling movies starring Errol Flynn, which Gilbert, Schafer and Grossman often watched for inspiration. They noticed that pirates in those films often taunted their opponents instead of attacking them, which gave the designers the idea to base the game's duels on insults rather than combat. Writer Orson Scott Card helped them write the insults during a visit to Lucasfilm's headquarters at Skywalker Ranch. Many of Gilbert's original gameplay ideas were abandoned during the production process, although he stated that "most of that stuff was left out for a reason".

cards.heading: Three trials on Mêlée Island
cards.text: A youth named Guybrush Threepwood arrives on Mêlée Island, hoping to become a pirate. He seeks out the island's pirate leaders, who set him three trials: winning a sword duel against Carla, the island's resident swordmaster; finding a buried treasure; and stealing a valuable idol from the governor's mansion. These quests take Guybrush throughout the island, where he hears of stories of the ghost pirate LeChuck, who apparently died in an expedition to the mysterious Monkey Island, an act that was meant to win the love of the governor, Elaine Marley. Guybrush meets several characters of interest, including a local voodoo priestess, Stan the Used Boat Salesman, Carla the Sword Master, a prisoner named Otis, and Meathook, whose hands have been replaced by hooks.

main.title: Dragon Quest IV
main.summary: Dragon Quest IV: Chapters of the Chosen, titled Dragon Warrior IV when initially localized to North America, is a 1990 role-playing video game, the fourth installment of the Dragon Quest video game series developed by Chunsoft and published by Enix, and the first of the Zenithian Trilogy.

cards.text: Dragon Quest IV: Chapters of the Chosen is a role-playing game developed by Chunsoft and published by Enix. Released for Famicom in Japan on 11 February 1990, it began the Zenithian trilogy. North America received it as Dragon Warrior IV for NES in October 1992, near the end of Enix America's period of publishing the series. Heartbeat later remade it for PlayStation. ArtePiazza brought that version to Nintendo DS in Japan in 2007 and internationally in 2008, with Android and iOS editions following in 2014.

Dragon Quest IV differs from the rest of the series by breaking up the game into five distinct chapters, each of which focuses on a different protagonist or protagonists. The first four are told from the perspective of the Hero's future companions and the fifth one, from the Hero's perspective, brings all the characters together as they start their journey to save the world. The remake adds a sixth chapter.

cards.heading: Companions make their own choices
cards.text: Dragon Quest IV lets companions choose their own actions during battle. In a 1989 interview, Yuji Horii and programmer Koichi Nakamura described the difficulty of balancing that independence with a useful role for the player. Choosing the strongest available response every time did not necessarily make a satisfying encounter. The team had to consider how the player could direct the group while its members acted for themselves.

cards.heading: The wagon changes the group
cards.text: Characters travelling in the wagon can gain experience while waiting outside overworld battles. Dungeons created a problem: companions left behind for too long could become too weak to return to the active party. Horii and Nakamura described allowing the wagon into some dungeons to address this. Where the group could travel determined which members remained practical choices later.

cards.heading: A village remembers the event
cards.text: In the later Dragon Quest VI interviews, Horii describes writing new town dialogue as events change. Returning to a village after becoming lost could produce another useful conversation instead of exactly the same response. The writing served the player's uncertain route through the world. A line was more than a small piece of exposition placed beside a house. Its availability depended on what had happened, and another version might be needed when the player returned with different knowledge and a different immediate problem.

cards.heading: The wrong person answers
cards.text: Programmer Manabu Yamana identifies a less glamorous difficulty: the party might reach an event in many different conditions. A townsperson calling for Hassan would create an awkward scene if Hassan were currently represented by a coffin. The software had to account for such possibilities. Dialogue and party rules could not be finished independently and joined without further work. A convincing conversation depended on checking who was actually present, what state they were in, and whether the words still made sense in that situation.

main.title: Crystalis
main.subtitle: SNK · Nintendo Entertainment System
main.summary: Crystalis is SNK's action role-playing adventure for the NES, set in a world recovering from a devastating war. A young man awakens without his memories and becomes involved in resistance to the Draygonian Empire. Villages, monsters and elemental magic occupy a landscape whose distant technological past gradually becomes important. The player explores from above, fighting directly while gathering equipment and experience. Its fantasy begins among familiar swords and sages, then connects those discoveries to the civilisation that left this changed world behind.

cards.heading: After the world has ended
cards.text: Crystalis is SNK's action role-playing adventure for the NES, set in a world recovering from a devastating war. A young man awakens without his memories and becomes involved in resistance to the Draygonian Empire. Villages, monsters and elemental magic occupy a landscape whose distant technological past gradually becomes important. The player explores from above, fighting directly while gathering equipment and experience. Its fantasy begins among familiar swords and sages, then connects those discoveries to the civilisation that left this changed world behind.

cards.heading: Choose the sword for the obstacle
cards.text: Four main swords carry the powers of wind, fire, water and thunder. Charging an attack releases an elemental projectile, and different enemies require different weapons. The same powers also change how the landscape can be crossed: the water sword can form ice bridges over suitable rivers, while other attacks remove barriers. Equipment therefore opens routes as well as improving combat. Returning to an earlier obstacle with another sword can reveal a way forward that was visible long before it was usable.

cards.heading: Strength grows alongside understanding
cards.text: Defeated monsters provide experience, raising the hero's level and combat strength. Some enemies require a sufficient level before they can be damaged, making equipment and experience complementary parts of preparation. Armour, shields, spells and useful items broaden the choices available on a journey. The original NES game later joined the SNK 40th Anniversary Collection, while a Game Boy Color adaptation appeared in 2000. The adventure's identity remains closely tied to its elemental weapons: each discovery changes both the next fight and the map around it.

main.title: Fire Emblem: Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light
main.summary: Fire Emblem: Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light, originally promoted simply as Fire Emblem, is a 1990 tactical role-playing video game developed by Intelligent Systems and Nintendo and published by Nintendo for the Family Computer.

cards.heading: Fire Emblem: Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light
cards.text: Fire Emblem: Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light, originally promoted simply as Fire Emblem, is a 1990 tactical role-playing video game developed by Intelligent Systems and Nintendo and published by Nintendo for the Family Computer. It is the first installment in the Fire Emblem series and was originally released in Japan. Set on the fictional continent of Archanea, the story follows the tale of Marth, prince of the kingdom of Altea, who is sent on a quest to reclaim his throne after being forced into exile by the evil sorcerer Gharnef and his dark master Medeus, the titular Shadow Dragon. Forming new alliances with neighboring kingdoms, Marth must gather a new army to help him retrieve the sacred sword Falchion and the Fire Emblem shield in order to defeat Gharnef and Medeus and save his kingdom. The gameplay revolves around turn-based battles on grid-based maps, with defeated units being subject to permanent death.

cards.heading: Strategy meets role-playing
cards.text: Beginning development in 1987, it was conceived by designer and writer Shouzou Kaga: influenced by Kure Software Koubou's First Queen (1988), Kaga wanted to combine the strategic elements of Intelligent Systems's previous simulation project, Famicom Wars, with the story, characters, and world of a traditional role-playing video game. Keisuke Terasaki acted as director and Gunpei Yokoi produced, while the music was composed by Yuka Tsujiyoko. The scale of the game meant that the team needed to find ways around memory storage problems, and make compromises with the graphics and storyline. While initial sales and critical reception were lackluster, it later became popular, launching the Fire Emblem series. The game would later be credited with codifying and popularizing the tactical role-playing genre as a whole.

cards.heading: The design
cards.text: The game was officially localized and released outside of Japan for the first time on the Nintendo Switch on December 4, 2020 in commemoration of the franchise's 30th anniversary. This updated version features new quality-of-life improvements such as fast-forwarding and rewinding through player and enemy turns, and the ability to create save states in the middle of gameplay. It was available digitally for a limited time until the end of March 2021.

main.title: Phantasy Star III: Generations of Doom
main.subtitle: An adventure across generations
main.summary: Phantasy Star III: Generations of Doom is Sega's role-playing game, first released for Mega Drive in Japan on 21 April 1990.

cards.heading: An adventure across generations
cards.text: Phantasy Star III: Generations of Doom is Sega's role-playing game, first released for Mega Drive in Japan on 21 April 1990. Prince Rhys sets out after his bride is abducted, beginning a journey that eventually passes to his descendants. Towns, dungeons and turn-based battles establish a familiar structure, while the story follows a family through three generations. The division between Orakians and Layans shapes the world the characters inherit. As the journey advances, marriage choices determine which descendants will become the heroes of its next part.

cards.heading: Choosing a family line
cards.text: At important points, the current protagonist chooses between two possible partners. The next generation then begins with another central character and a different combination of inherited circumstances and abilities. Two possible second-generation protagonists lead to four possible heroes in the third generation. Replaying the story can therefore reveal another family line rather than simply repeat the same party's adventure. The choice connects the larger conflict to individual relationships, making the people travelling together matter to the structure of the campaign as well as its immediate battles.

cards.heading: The world inherited
cards.text: Exploration moves between settlements and dangerous areas, with encounters shifting the party into menu-driven combat. Icons organise commands, and an automatic battle option can handle routine exchanges. The changing cast gives the player new combinations to learn as the generations succeed one another. Developed by a different team from its predecessors, the game gave the series a distinct narrative experiment. Its most memorable idea lies in that passage of time: the protagonist who begins the adventure leaves behind a world, and a family, for somebody else to continue exploring.

main.title: Magician Lord
main.subtitle: One of Neo Geo’s first worlds
main.summary: Magician Lord is Alpha Denshi's side-scrolling action game, first released for Neo Geo MVS in Japan on 26 April 1990.

cards.heading: One of Neo Geo’s first worlds
cards.text: Magician Lord is Alpha Denshi's side-scrolling action game, first released for Neo Geo MVS in Japan on 26 April 1990. Elta, a descendant of an earlier magician, crosses Cadacis to recover eight grimoires and prevent a destructive power from returning. Magic shots, platforming and doors into dangerous chambers form the journey. As one of the first Neo Geo arcade releases and an early home-console pack-in, it helped introduce the hardware through large, colourful fantasy scenes. Its central ability lets Elta become a different creature by collecting elemental orbs.

cards.heading: Two orbs, another body
cards.text: Fire, water and wind orbs combine in pairs to create six transformations. A dragon warrior breathes fire, a water-based form attacks along the ground, and other combinations produce fighters with different projectiles or jumping abilities. Choosing and preserving a form changes how Elta handles the next stretch of the stage. The transformation also expands his health, making it protection as well as another weapon. A useful combination can therefore make an intimidating room more manageable, provided the player can avoid losing it before reaching the next major encounter.

cards.heading: Power that can be lost
cards.text: Each stage includes doors leading through trap-filled areas towards a miniboss and the final boss guarding a grimoire. Treasure chests supply points, power-ups and the orbs needed for transformation. Taking damage can reduce Elta's attack power and eventually return him to his ordinary body, so strength remains something to protect. Hideki Yamamoto, Hiroaki Shimizu and Yuka Watanabe composed the score. The colourful forms and imposing enemies gave the early Neo Geo a memorable display, while the demanding route made control of that power central to surviving it.

main.title: Final Fantasy III
main.summary: Final Fantasy III is a 1990 role-playing video game developed and published by Square for the Family Computer.

cards.text: Final Fantasy III is a 1990 role-playing video game developed and published by Square for the Family Computer. The third installment in the Final Fantasy series, it follows four orphans from the village of Ur who are chosen by the world's crystals to defeat a great evil and return balance to the world. The gameplay returns to the traditional combat system of the original game, and adds a job system allowing players to switch between character classes with unique abilities.

Development of Final Fantasy III was handled by multiple series veterans including director Hironobu Sakaguchi, designers Hiromichi Tanaka and Kazuhiko Aoki, writer Kenji Terada, composer Nobuo Uematsu, and programmer Nasir Gebelli in his final contribution to the series. Production was a struggle due to data management, and new elements were added to encourage player experimentation. The artwork was a collaborative effort between Koichi Ishii as character and job designer, Yoshitaka Amano as monster designer, and Kazuko Shibuya as main sprite artist. When it completed development, it was described as one of the largest games on the system.

Upon its release in Japan, the game sold 1.4 million copies, and saw generally positive reviews, with most of the praise going to its job system. While ported to multiple platforms in later years, the original was not released outside Japan until 2021. A remake for the WonderSwan Color was planned but ultimately cancelled, while a 3D remake for the Nintendo DS was released internationally in 2006. The game saw the introduction of several recurring elements including a job system, summoned monsters and the Moogle. Terada also adapted it into a manga, and its characters and settings made appearances in later Final Fantasy titles.

cards.heading: A landscape made from repetitions
cards.text: Kazuko Shibuya remembers making the first Final Fantasy's opening landscape under a severe memory limit. A complete new picture would not fit. Hills and sea reused small graphic elements, sometimes flipped to vary their appearance, while the foreground became a black silhouette. The solution kept the travelers readable without supplying every surface with new detail. In her 2013 account, the memorable image grew from choices about what to repeat and what to leave empty, rather than from an unrestricted illustration reduced to screen size.

cards.heading: A drawing is not a sprite
cards.text: Shibuya recalled that the internal team created the playable characters while some monsters began with Yoshitaka Amano's monochrome drawings. Translating those drawings to the screen required further choices about a limited palette. Other staff, including Shibuya herself, also designed monsters. Illustration, character design and sprite production contributed different work to the finished images.

cards.heading: A planner learns the tool
cards.text: Koichi Ishii describes another route into the same craft. During the first Final Fantasy, Shibuya was occupied with Rad Racer, so he asked Takashi Tokita to teach him the sprite tools. His first attempt disappeared because he saved it incorrectly. Eventually a working side-view battle display persuaded Hironobu Sakaguchi to use that approach for the characters. Ishii recalls continuing to adjust individual pixels himself. Planning a character, learning a tool and judging an animated result happened together, rather than as neatly separated departments.

cards.heading: Colour carries a role
cards.text: For Final Fantasy III, Ishii wanted each job to have its own pose and imagined background. A small palette made those differences difficult. Instead of always reserving one colour for skin, he experimented with bright yellow, khaki and blue to find another family of characters. For the first game, he describes arranging black marks in white mountains for the colour effects produced by a CRT television. The intended picture included the display's behaviour. A sharp modern view can therefore show different relationships from the image these artists were composing.
